subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT ENABLING ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED TO CARRY OUT ENGINEERING ASSESSMENT OF DEUTERIUM PLANT

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT ENABLING ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED TO CARRY OUT ENGINEERING ASSESSMENT OF DEUTERIUM PLANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that the government has authorized Atomic Energy of Canada Limited to enter into an agreement with Deuterium of Canada Limited and the government of Nova Scotia to enable Atomic Energy of Canada Limited to carry out an engineering assessment to determine the feasibility and probable costs of bringing the Deuterium plant at Glace Bay into production.
The province of Nova Scotia and Deuterium of Canada Limited have a very substantial investment in this venture, and its failure would be a serious financial setback for the province of Nova Scotia.
The province has indicated to the government that it is not practicable, because of the lack of sufficient technical expertise at the provincial level, for the province to bring the plant into production and operate it with its own provincial facilities and resources. The government has therefore authorized the above study, which does not include any commitment on the part of the federal government or AECL to carry out further work or to put the plant into production or to operate same, but which study will be submitted to the government for its consideration upon completion.
The study will be embarked upon and completed at the earliest possible date, and AECL has been authorized to spend the sum of $300,000 of its own funds toward such study.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):

Officials of Atomic Energy of Canada have always been most helpful, and I am pleased to see that this degree of co-operation is evidently continuing. I express the hope that this study and other efforts will lead to an early solution of the problems since this is obviously of great importance to the province of Nova Scotia and indeed to the country as a whole.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT ENABLING ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED TO CARRY OUT ENGINEERING ASSESSMENT OF DEUTERIUM PLANT

I agree with the minister that the amount of knowledge on the provincial level is not adequate to deal with this type of problem. I think it can be more properly done by Atomic Energy of Canada Limit-

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT ENABLING ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED TO CARRY OUT ENGINEERING ASSESSMENT OF DEUTERIUM PLANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I am quite familiar with the problem of the heavy water plant in Glace Bay, I am pleased to make some comments on the minister's statement.
What surprises me is that the federal government wants to assist a Crown corporation established by the former premier of Nova Scotia who is now Leader of the official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). This corporation, as we know, is on the verge of bankruptcy. It is a white elephant. It has shown only deficits since the beginning and it costs several million dollars in interests alone.
We know quite well that the leader of the Liberal party in Nova Scotia based its election campaign last year on the possibility of saving the heavy water plant. Now, that plant is completely obsolete and we want to save, at a cost of $300,000, an undertaking that is considered in Nova Scotia as nothing more than a white elephant. Moreover, until now the company has been very badly managed financially.
I wonder how come the federal government now wants to risk an amount of $300,000, unless it is to keep the election promise of the present premier of Nova Scotia, and also to save an undertaking launched by the Leader of the official Opposition, a crown company on the verge of bankruptcy that has never produced an ounce of heavy water to this day.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL RE-ORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Thursday, January 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Drury (for the Prime Minister) that Bill C-207, respecting the organization of the government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto, be read the second time and referred to a committee of the whole.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL RE-ORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
When I was speaking yesterday evening, I expressed my astonishment at the fact that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) in introducing this bill had suggested that if passed it would enhance the control of Parliament over the executive. I had, by way of illustration to counter his astonishing statement, made some reference to the proposed department of environment. I suggested that this department had already been created by Order in Council and that, therefore, to ask us now to approve its establishment was making a mockery of the concept of the control of Parliament over the executive, rather than the reverse. A few fancy bits of verbiage and a new name do not in any way alter the substance of what

the government has already done by Order in Council under the authority of the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act.
I think it is pertinent to this debate that we should dust off this Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act. It appears to have been on our statute books for a long while. It has not been amended since the Revised Statutes of 1952, and if I read it correctly there, it was taken intact from the Revised Statutes of 1927. I have not pursued its history further back than that. It has only two sections in addition to the Title. I submit it is time we took a look at its terms in detail, and that in fact it should be part of the record of the discussion on this government organization bill. So, I would like to quote from it. Section 2 of the act reads:
The Governor in Council may (a) transfer any powers, duties or functions or the control or supervision of any part of the public service from one Minister of the Crown to any other Minister of the Crown, or from one department or portion of the public service to any other department or portion of the public service: or (b) amalgamate and combine any two or more departments under one Minister of the Crown and under one deputy minister.
Section 3 reads:
Whenever under the provisions of this Act, or under any other lawful authority, any power, duty or function, or the control or supervision of any part of the public service is transferred from one Minister of the Crown to any other Minister of the Crown, or from one department or branch of the public service to any other department or branch of the public service, the Minister, department or branch to which the power, duty, function, control or supervision is transferred, and the appropriate officers of that department or branch, shall, in relation thereto, be substituted for and have and may exercise the respective powers and duties that formerly belonged to or were exercisable by the minister, department or branch and the respective officers of the department or branch from which the power, duty, function, control or supervision is so transferred as aforesaid.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, that is the complete text of that act which has been sitting on our statute books for a long while.
It is important in this context because, as the President of the Treasury Board himself said in his introductory speech the government, in latter years, had been making increasingly wide use of the powers which are conferred by this statute. In fact, Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out last night the department for which it is proposed to substitute the new department of environment was, in fact, created in this way, as I indicated by making a reference to the introduction to the first annual report of the Department of Fisheries and Forestry. So, I think it is quite pertinent that we should examine the situation in respect of the government organization bills which are becoming an annual event in the sessions of this Parliament.
If, in fact, we were being asked to repeal, or amend, or alter the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act, so as to reduce the authority of the government to move segments of the public service about at will from one part of the ministry to another, then I suppose the veracity of the statement made by the President of the Treasury Board would be emphasized but,
January 29, 1971

Mr. Speaker, that is not what we are being asked to do. I suggest that the debate on this bill is well focused upon the question of just what direction we are heading in relation to the whole question of the authority of the executive to manage the public service and the authority, if any, that Parliament should be able to exercise.
In considering this question I thought I would put forward a form of a bill which I think perhaps actually represents more closely the real state of affairs at this moment than does the exercise which the government has proposed for us in the government organization bill that we are debating. I would like to suggest this as an appropriate statement of the actual state of affairs which currently exists as far as the relationship between the parliamentary branch and the executive branch of the government of Canada is concerned, and in particular with reference to the developing position of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the picture, which has been touched upon by some of the other speakers in this debate. So, Mr. Speaker, this is a draft bill. It reads:
An Act respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto.
Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
Shobt Title
1.	This Act may be cited as the Act to End Government Organization Acts, 1971.
Part I
Department of the Prime Minister
2.	(1) There shall be a Government of Canada called the Department of the Prime Minister over which the member of the Queen's Privy Council holding the recognized position of First Minister shall preside.
(2) The Prime Minister holds office during his own pleasure and has the management and direction of the Department of the Prime Minister.
3.	The Governor in Council may appoint an officer called the Deputy Minister of the Prime Minister to be deputy head of the Department of the Prime Minister and to hold office during pleasure.
4.	The duties, powers and functions of the Prime Minister extend to and include all matters over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction, not by law assigned to any other government.
Past II
Sub-Departments
5.	The Prime Minister may from time to time establish such Sub-Departments as he sees fit and shall assign to them such titles as he deems appropriate, and may abolish such SubDepartments or change their titles or functions at his pleasure.
6.	(1) The Prime Minister shall appoint from amongst other members of the Privy Council a Sub-Minister to preside over each sub-department, to hold office during pleasure.
(2)	Each Sub-Minister shall exercise such powers, and perform such duties and functions as may be assigned to him under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act.
(3)	The Prime Minister shall not, pursuant to sub-section (1) appoint Sub-ministers so that there are more than fifty such sub-ministers in existence at any one time.
7.	The Governor in Council may appoint an officer called a Sub-Deputy Minister to be deputy head of each sub-department.
Government Organization Act, 1970
Paht hi
Transitional and Consequential
8.	Without restricting the generality of section 2, the Acts to be administered by the Prime Minister include the Acts set out in Schedule A, and whenever any department, minister or deputy minister is mentioned or referred to in any of those Acts, or in any order, rule or regulation made thereunder, or any contract, lease, licence or other document made or issued pursuant thereto, there shall in every case, unless the context otherwise requires, be substituted the Department of the Prime Minister, The Prime Minister, or the Deputy Minister of the Prime Minister, as the case may be.
9.	This Act shall come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation at the pleasure of the Prime Minister.
Schedule A.
Every Act heretofore or hereinafter enacted.
You may have recognized, Mr. Speaker, that I have put forward this proposal with tongue in cheek. I have done so to emphasize the point that, for all practical purposes, my proposal represents very closely the actual state of affairs in our governmental system at present. If we are to consider the realities of the situation, perhaps we ought to consider the form as well. Parliament ought not to be asked to go annually through this exercise, as we are now being asked to participate in this debate, unless this House is to have some real authority over the nature of what government departments shall be brought into being from time to time. In the absence of that authority, I think we should simply recognize that this matter lies entirely within the prerogative of the executive and in the hands of the Prime Minister, and be done with it. At least that would give us a greater opportunity for assessing and discussing real legislative proposals upon which the operations of the government must hinge.
There are bills before us that have substance and that will have an impact on the future. We passed several during the previous session. For example, the Canada Water Act is the kind of bill that will affect the future operations of the government in relation to the welfare of the Canadian people. Unless the government can agree, when dealing with such questions as organization, to place before Parliament propositions of significance and meaning which Parliament can debate and decide in order to give real guidance to the course the government should take in the organization of the operations of the public service, we ought to have done with the kind of mockery we are witnessing now. Instead of discussing a fait accompli with regard, for example, to the establishment of a department of the environment, we ought to have the opportunity, if the government believes that Parliament should have the power to direct some general trends of government organization, of expressing ourselves on the basic concept before the department is established and not after it has been created. That, Mr. Speaker, is the meat of this debate, especially when one looks at the matter in the light of the terms which were set out by the President of the Treasury Board in his initial remarks.

January 29, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
Debate might be more real or meaningful if the government were to introduce in resolution from the concept underlying the setting up of a new department or underlying the division of the operations of the government. I made a rough draft of the kind of resolution that might be considered in the context of the current debate. If, before action was taken under the Transfer of Duties Act to create the department of the environment, we had been given the opportunity of telling the government what we thought the nature of that department ought to be, what general areas of operation it ought to be involved in and what jurisdiction it ought to exercise and then perhaps allow the government to look after the details of transfers of branches or subbranches in order to build the appropriate organization based on a concept approved by Parliament, and if a resolution along the lines I shall read in a minute had been introduced in the previous session and agreed to by the House, then, I suggest, not too much criticism could have been levelled at the transfer, for example of the wildlife service from one ministry to the new department of the environment.
In order to emphasize my feelings on this matter, Mr. Speaker, I should like to suggest that the House might have adopted a resolution along the following lines:
Resolved:
That there he established a Ministry of the Environment, with duties, powers and functions extending, within the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada, over renewable resources and the protection and enhancement of the quality of the natural environment, including water, air and soil quality; such duties and powers to include the implementation and administration of all relevant legislation enacted by Parliament, including that related to water, fisheries, forests, migratory birds and other wild animal and plant life; And be it further resolved: that the appropriate existing branches and agencies within the Public Service be transferred to, and co-ordinated within the proposed Ministry of the Environment.
If we had been given an opportunity to participate in a debate on such a resolution before the establishment of the department, instead of after, we could have embarked on a really meaningful debate in Parliament which could have been of value in guiding the government on the details of its organization. For example, in view of the overlapping in certain areas of government, we could have discussed whether any elements or government organizations dealing with the soil of Canada ought to be removed from the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture and placed under the jurisdiction of the new department. We could have embarked on a meaningful debate over the question of whether the management of the commercial fisheries of Canada ought to remain the responsibility of the ministry of fisheries or be transferred to the ministry of the environment. We could have debated the question of whether the parks branch should remain within the rather strange, existing structures of the Department of Indians Affairs and Northern Development, or whether it might more appropriately come within the department of the environment. The Parks branch now seems to be a sort of appendage to the department headed by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien). If we are increasingly to use our present methods, what is the
point in even bothering to go through this kind of hollow exercise which deals only with the outer shell and not with the meat of the change in government structure and organization. I think it is time for Parliament to indicate that we ought to call a halt to the present trend in government actions.
Although I have not consulted the relevant debates, I imagine that the Transfer of Duties Act was intended to be used for the sort of minor transfer arrangements that create some flexibility in the operations of government. I am quite sure that the parliamentarians who agreed to the passage of that bill, and who put it on our statute books, did not envisage that one day the executive, of its own accord, would use the authority of that law to create out of the blue entirely new departments embracing new concepts of government. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge hon. members of the House to consider the implications of what we did this year, last year, the year before that and the year before that, in dealing with omnibus bills relating to government organization.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL RE-ORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a great many members on this side of the House have already voiced their objections to this kind of omnibus bill. It is not my intention to repeat what has been said. However, I wish to state that I agree with the position of my colleagues in this party and members of other opposition parties. The basic problem is that hon. members, including government members, are faced with the situation, as the old expression goes, of having to throw out the baby with the bath water. In other words, there are many things in this bill that should be separated. I cannot understand why the government would not like to have on the record the unanimous support of the House on some aspects of this bill. On the other hand, there are some sections of this bill which a great many members, including government members, may not wholeheartedly support.
With regard to the phrase the "baby and the bathwater", the baby part of the bill deals with the new department of the environment. I think all hon. members are generally in favour of that, particularly in view of the fact that it will come under the auspices of one of the better ministers of the cabinet. No government is all bad. There are some good ministers in the present cabinet. Certainly, the minister who is proposed to head this new department is in this category.
The matter of having the whole problem of pollution under one department has been promoted by my colleagues for approximately a year. Perhaps the government does sometimes pay attention to suggestions from the opposition. If so, we welcome that. It is ridiculous to have some aspects of pollution under the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis), some aspects under the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), some under the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) and some under the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene). The federal government is very limited in what it can do with regard to

January 29, 1971

pollution. It is very gratifying to learn that the authority, and resulting co-ordination, will at least come under one minister, a very capable minister at that.
Having dealt with the baby, I now wish to deal with the bathwater part of the bill. The bathwater part of the bill deals with the creation of ministers of the state, Parliamentary Secretaries and the like.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL RE-ORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is pretty dirty water.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL RE-ORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Our rules of Parliament are properly designed so that we cannot impute motives to individuals in this House. No one really knows what is going on inside someone else's head. Sometimes they do not know themselves. Knowing the background of this present session of Parliament, a reasonable person could only reach one conclusion. By means of this omnibus bill, the government is indirectly attempting to do something that it does not want to do directly. When the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was asked what the just society meant, he said "just for grits". The legislation before us amply justifies that remark.
As hon. members are aware, suggestions have been made at various times that the government might do something about increasing the salaries and allowances of members of this House. Because the suggestions were not adequately presented to the public, they met with considerable resistance. This is chiefly because the public have not been made aware of the expenses and costs faced by members of this House. This is one of the weaknesses of Information Canada. However, that is another matter. Apparently the government is not anxious to present legislation to increase members' salaries at the present time. Some members opposite asked what could be done to get government members off the hook, and to forget about the opposition members. This bill is evidence of what is happening.
This bill recommends the appointment of five additional ministers of state. As I understand the bill, they will receive an additional $15,000 a year. That is pretty good. At the present time there are 28 cabinet ministers. If this bill is passed, there will be 33. As far as I know, there is nothing to prevent the Prime Minister from appointing an additional number of ministers without portfolio who will receive an additional $7,500 per year. It is also suggested that there be as many Parliamentary Secretaries as ministers. They will receive an additional $4,000 per year. This is a very interesting arrangement. If and when this legislation is passed, there will be 33 ministers of state and ministers without portfolio, and 33 Parliamentary Secretaries for a total of 66. In addition, there are 25 committee chairmen.
At the moment, these committee chairmen do not receive an additional stipend, only a title. However, they may eventually receive more. According to what we hear, there is considerable stirring among the backbench government members. They can hardly be blamed because, at the time of the last election, many were persuaded to run on the basis that eventually there would be an increase in the stipend or something else
Government Organization Act, 1970 would be forthcoming. It is easy to understand how this bill came about.
In the past, people have accused the Prime Minister of having socialist inclinations. I do not agree with that. In view of this legislation, the Prime Minister must be a prime promoter of good, old-fashioned capitalism and incentives. The creation of additional ministers of state, ministers without portfolio and Parliamentary Secretaries, is a wonderful way of keeping people under control. If a member of the government is a good boy and has some ability, he will be made a minister of state. If he is not quite as good, he might be made a minister without portfolio. If a member behaves and keeps his nose clean, he may become a Parliamentary Secretary. If he is bad, he may be made a committee chairman with no additional money, only a bit of honour. If he is really bad, he will be put in the sin bin and not receive anything extra. That is the way it goes. It is fairly easy to switch Parliamentary Secretaries on the excuse that everyone should have the opportunity of showing their wares. This is a good idea. It also brings in a good income.
Many people have the uneasy feeling that by introducing this bill the government is establishing a device to reward government members with extra income and at the same time ensuring that opposition members do not receive anything extra. This is a sort of Machiavellian way of doing things. It is to be expected. We do not know where this idea originated. Undoubtedly, there are members opposite who are capable of thinking of such things. It is nice for members to have titles and extra money. It is nice to have the title of a Privy Councillor so that when you leave this House you can put the initials P.C. after your name.
The Prime Minister was apparently a good student. He must have spent a good deal of time reading about a man who was a dictator in Haiti for a good many years, Henri Christophe, who met a very sad fate. He died with a silver bullet in his head. He had a very interesting way of dealing with things. He liked to have a lot of flatterers around him, but he did not have the money to pay them. Unlike the present government, he did not have the means of extracting money from the people. He gave all these people round him titles. He did not call them ministers of state, nothing as pedestrian as that. Mr. Speaker, I am not making this up, this is on the record. He called people the Duke and Duchess of Lemonade, the Count of Sugar Cane and the like. I am rather surprised that the Prime Minister, with his inventive mind, did not think of something like this for the members of this Parliament. He could easily have appointed somebody from London, Ontario as the Baron of Blizzard, or somebody from the Windsor or Sarnia area could have been given the title of Prince of Pollution or something of that type. I am surprised that he did not do this in view of his inventiveness and imagination.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL RE-ORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
What about the Marquis of Maple Syrup?

January 29, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL RE-ORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
That is a good suggestion from the hon. member for Renfrew-Lanark-Carleton (Mr. McBride) the Marquis of Maple Syrup. Perhaps he would like to have that title; it is nice and sugary. Perhaps my thinking is not as accurate as it might be in this regard, but in view of the evidence I do not see how anybody could come to any other reasonable conclusion.
Let us consider the remainder of this bill. We have dealt with the watery portions of the bill. There is a great deal of verbiage, a lot of shifting and shuffling of cabinet ministers and those areas falling within their jurisdictions. I think it is probably a good idea that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) has been given responsibility for everything that could be sold. I think this is probably a good idea. I hope the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) will remain in the same position so we will not have people in manpower offices all around the country receiving advice from other ministers. Most of this shuffling and shifting that is going on reminds me of the old shell and pea game we used to see at county fairs; first you see the pea and then you don't.
The government has become worried about the image of the Prime Minister as created by the public relations people. It has now become apparent that, in fact, what has happened has been that, to paraphrase Mr. Marshall McLuhan, logic has become mystery. I should like to change that slightly and refer to the attitude of the government as being one in which shadow has become substance. The government is great in this field. It always presents what it intends to do by doctoring up these shadows and presenting them as substance. This is merely an example of shadow and substance being the same.
We have heard a great deal about participatory democracy. Much of this image has been created by Information Canada and other government agencies. The government does not accept suggestions from this side of the House. Members on the government side feel that no one on this side has any good ideas. The acceptance of a suggestion from this side seems to be considered by the government as a sign of weakness, unless there is a great deal of pressure accompanying the suggestion.
I am surprised that the government did not take advantage of the omnibus bill to accept and implement the idea of an ombudsman. As everyone in this House knows, this idea has worked very well in a number of other countries including Finland, Sweden, New Zealand and others. I understand it has worked very well in Alberta, and I am surprised the government has not accepted the idea. The more a central government becomes involved in various aspects of human life, the more it alienates citizens from government authority. An ombudsman would do a great deal to alleviate this situation.
I was looking over a number of files I have in my office. I discovered one in respect of a widow of a serviceman in the Royal Canadian Navy. He was killed two or three years ago as a result of the greatest possible negligence on the part of authorities on the ship on
which he was serving. His widow was denied any account of what actually took place and she was unable to take appropriate action against the Crown. This woman had a number of children and there is apparently no remedy for her situation.
I have another file respecting an elderly lady in my own city who slipped on ice on the Post Office steps and was seriously injured. A representative of the Public Works Department who was employed there came around and told her that the ice should not have been on the steps. He said she had a valid complaint and she should put her complaint in the mail within a week. She accepted that advice and did so. The government of that day, which was the same party in power today, said she had not sent in a formal notice and was not entitled to any compensation.
I have another file in my hand in respect of a man in the Armed Forces who was badly injured while on duty. He tried to obtain compensation but the Department of National Defence refused to give him anything. I am sure every Member of Parliament could cite examples of this kind of thing. This is further evidence in support of the need for the appointment of an ombudsman. An ombudsman would get right to the seat of the difficulty, which results from the bureaucracy of the civil service, and would put a stop to the infernal policies of secrecy adopted by every branch of organized government.
Let me cite an example of this secrecy which came to light as a result of a letter I received two days ago from a constituent. He is a druggist in the city in which I five. I do not think he is an admirer of the present government but he said he was glad to find that the present government was very anxious to keep its correspondence clear, concise and untroubled. In an open letter which was enclosed in an envelope from the Department of National Health and Welfare was a sheet of paper with absolutely nothing on it. Apparently, this represents the policy of secrecy.
This policy of secrecy applies in many other ways. Perhaps by referring again to Haiti I can make my point. The government there was attempting to change some of the directives of Papa Doc Duvalier. This type of thing is taking place apparently in respect of government organizations or agencies such as Air Canada. We have heard evidence of the use of electronic devices to determine the efficiency of its employees in the two official languages. This is a rather shocking type of inspection.
When I first came into this House a Liberal government was in power. At that time that government attempted to use the same techniques in respect of post office employees. Television cameras were installed in the washrooms in the post office at Peterborough. I cannot imagine what the purpose was, but it was suggested that the government wanted to find out whether people were stealing things. After a great deal of pressure was applied, the government was forced to abandon this project. I certainly hope that this kind of behaviour and activity will cease forthwith.
Other examples of government secrecy have been apparent in this House in the last couple of days. My

January 29, 1971

hon. friends to my left are always asking for the production of papers. I do not recall more than one or two instances during this session of Parliament when these requests have been accepted. It certainly is not the custom of this government to give out information respecting memoranda between departments. Everyone knows that this sort of thing is taking place and that the government makes a fetish of secrecy. This reminds me of my association with the Department of External Affairs when junior foreign service officers made a great thing of placing a high degree of classification on all information. It seems to me it is very dangerous to treat everything as being secret. It is like the boy who cried wolf. Sometimes when you really want to keep something secret people treat it with carelessness, and this is the only result of trying to keep everything secret. I suggest some steps should have been taken by the government in this bill to try to prevent this complete hiding of all information, even of the most trivial and inconsequential nature, from the people of Canada, not to mention members of the opposition whose job it is, under our parliamentary system, to criticize the mistakes of government and offer solutions or alternative methods.
Another thing the government should have done but did not is this. We have had enough complaints, even complaints from members on the government side, about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I do not want to elaborate on this matter; I have said enough about it in the House over the years. However, I do want to say that it is apparently the accepted pattern of behaviour in public affairs broadcasts made by the corporation for individuals to use these public facilities, which are made available to them at great cost to the public, as an instrument to try to brainwash the people of Canada by expressing their own particular political, personal and economic views.
I do not have to enlarge on this because every member of the House knows that this sort of thing is done regularly. Members on both sides of the House have been very anxious to put some kind of control on those using the facilities of that organization to promote their own political, personal and economic philosophies. Many things could be done, but one suggestion is that we establish a parliamentary committee, on which no party is dominant, which could entertain complaints made by the public and others and then make recommendations to the CBC.
Then, there is the related matter of controlling actions emanating from government commissions. Certainly, from what we have heard this week some control needs to be exercised over the Public Service Commission. The Unemployment Insurance Commission has been having a grand time during the last few years conducting a virtual reign of terror among various sections of the public, interpretating the act in its own way. The commission follows the pattern in, "Alice in Wonderland", being both judge and jury. This can be said not only of this commission but of most government commissions.
Government Organization Act, 1970
These commissions were set up with the very best of intentions. There was to be no political interference. Although I have heard suggestions in former days with regard to the public service, I have never found any great evidence of interference. All of these commissions and crown corporations like the CNR, Air Canada and so on, were set up on the understanding there was to be no political interference. But once you have created a Frankenstein monster, which in theory is responsible to Parliament as a whole, you in fact have created a monster that is responsible to no one.
As any hon. member who has been in this House for some time well knows, there is no way you can deal with the administration of these commissions, even though they are public emanations. The public pays $180 million a year to maintain the CBC. I am not suggesting that members of parliament should be allowed to meddle in the running of crown corporations, but I do suggest there should be some degree of control by the House in actual practice.
Perhaps an arrangement similar to what I have suggested for the CBC would be workable, but it is clear that something must be done to control the activities of some corporations. I think the government would be the first to welcome this suggestion, in view of the action taken by the Public Service Commission during the last few days-at least if what the government says is true. Only this morning the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) suggested in the House that something must be done to make crown corporations such as the CNR and Air Canada conform to public policy, particularly as it relates to unemployment at the present time. Only a few moments ago members on the government side gave a round of applause to the hon. member for that suggestion, indicating their support, and I give him my support as well.
Another step that could be taken would be the improvement of the committee system of Parliament. A new committee system was introduced a couple of years ago with high hopes. To be perfectly fair, a great many government members of these committees have exhibited a great deal of independence and have put forward some very good ideas. But what has happened to the committees' reports? I was a member of the transportation committee at the time the committee went on an expensive junket to look into Maritime transportation problems. But before the committee had returned to Ottawa the government had acted on some of the matters the committee was considering.
The defence committee took a two or three week trip to Cyprus, West Germany, Sweden, to hell's half acre one might say, and submitted what was almost an unanimous report on defence policy. Although this report was supported by most government members, again it was completely disregarded by the government. Then, suggestions were made by the veterans committee, and there was the notorious incident with the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development whose unanimous suggestion was ignored.
Now, everybody knows that no government can be expected to accept every report of every committee; that

January 29, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
would be clearly ridiculous. But it does seem that some arrangement should be made to oblige the government to pay some attention to reports made by committees, particularly unanimous reports. The government's attitude has a very bad effect on Parliament as a whole. Those members who work very hard on committees, and spend long hours devoting their attention to them, are treated like children playing house. If committees are merely a means of keeping people occupied around here, then this situation is not satisfactory.
Another matter that should have been dealt with in the bill, and which I will not deal with at length, is limiting the staff and expenses of cabinet ministers. Since we now have a cabinet that is about three times as big as it was previously, some limit should be placed on expenses. I remember some years ago one cabinet minister-I am not going to mention his name because that would not be proper, but if hon. members want to know they can see me afterwards privately-who had his office redecorated about four times in one year. He had a gold coloured rug on the floor, gold handles on his door and all that sort of thing. There is no excuse for this. If we are going to have a multiplicity of cabinet appointments, then something should be done to limit expenses.
My final suggestion relates to a most important matter. Members on both sides of the House have talked about our youth. Some say youth is bad, others say that it has never had a chance. We hear references to the generation gap and to other trite expressions. But no one to my knowledge ever does anything about youth. I asked a question about the plans for student employment this summer, and I was told that the government was formulating plans and getting around to dealing with that matter. Apparently responsibility has been divided between the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang). It is the old story of too many cooks not only spoiling the broth but not making any broth at all.
It seems to me that the government has missed a glorious opportunity here. I hope that before this bill receives second reading the government will consider withdrawing it and accepting some of the suggestions made by members on this side of the House. The government can then bring in a bill all of us can be proud of, one which would greatly assist future operations of this or any other government.
Therefore, I hope the government gives serious consideration to establishing a department of youth. I do not refer to some phony department that does not do anything but to one that would really turn its attention to two very important matters, one of which may well affect the basic future of Canada, especially during the next 25 to 30 years. To a certain degree, this suggestion had been adopted by a minister of the previous Liberal government, Miss LaMarsh. I was not always an admirer of Miss LaMarsh, but in this case she did something very good. During centennial year she arranged for young people from all provinces to travel across Canada. They

were able to visit in other provinces for a few days. Nothing could have been more valuable in terms of the future of this country. Young people, for example from Quebec, had an opportunity to visit Saskatchewan and vice versa and young people from southern Ontario had an opportunity to visit Newfoundland. One thing is certain. Twenty-five years from now the people who now are in the age bracket between 12 and 20 will be running this country. If these people live in virtual isolation they might develop many built-in prejudices. They might have suspicions in respect of what people in other parts of Canada are trying to do against them. Such things are bound to arise in a country such as ours with its great distances.
One problem Canada has always had has involved the suspicion the English and French-speaking members of the population have had of one another. This is only natural. If people are unable to communicate there is bound to be suspicion. There is enough suspicion between the Maritimes and Ontario about economic problems and yet the people speak the same language. However, when we have the additional problem of language, the situation becomes worse. One way to get around this difficulty is by helping the young people move around the country so that they will have an opportunity to talk to each other. In my area we have had students from all parts of Canada visit us on an exchange basis. Nothing could be better for the future of our country. At the present time, when large numbers of high school and university students are out of work, it would be money well spent- instead of pouring it down the drain in respect of the CBC and some other institutions.

to provide funds so that these young people could travel. I do not suggest that the arrangements should be elaborate. The young people I know would not want this.
The young people would like an opportunity to visit other parts of the country. If we could help them do this we would be performing a real service to our country and its future. The young people would be occupied in this way rather than being influenced by the rabble rousers who are not interested in what is good for the future of Canada. We know that last year many of our young people were on the highways without proper food and the other necessities. One can expect people to be resentful about this. This is a plan the government might consider implementing this summer, in view of the unemployment situation which faces our young people. They might not earn any money in this way but at least they would get a wonderful appreciation of what our country is and could be.
There is one final comment I should like to make. I believe that not only the young people of our country- and I get around every year to all the high schools in my area-but also many of the middle-aged and older people have no real idea how Parliament or our government operates. I do not know how we can expect the average citizen to respect this institution when he has little knowledge concerning how it works. So far as I am concerned, no adequate book has been written on the subject of how Parliament operates. Most people think
January 29, 1971

that members sit here all day listening to golden words or little pearls of wisdom. When a debate is in progress, such as is the case now, they say that hardly anyone is present. We all know the reasons for this, but the public does not know or does not understand. Frequently, we are compared to the United States. You can bet your bottom dollar every young person in the United States knows how the Congress works, how the committee system works and what the powers of the President are. Very few people in Canada have any idea how our system of government works.
Perhaps the government, with the co-operation of the provinces, the CBC, and through the use of pamphlets and the press could help our young people understand how our democratic parliamentary system works and why it is not necessary to go to the streets in order to put ideas across. So many people say that nobody pays any attention to them. They say the country is undemocratic and that they have to take to the streets. That idea is promoted by people in Canada for their own ends. Many people have no idea how parliamentary democracy works or how the cabinet system works. This situation must be changed if we expect the country to flourish in the future. If the educational system of our country, in the hands of the provinces, is not working in this regard something must be done to make it work. Our system of government has been worked out over the centuries. It is a very flexible system. Something must be done so that future Canadians will appreciate and understand it. If this is not done, then anything else that is done in this House will be of little value to the future of our country.
I hope the government will make some appropriate changes in this bill so that it might incorporate some of the suggestions which not only I have made but which other hon. members have made and probably will make within the next few days.

Undoubtedly so. If this bill is passed, we will have a few extra ministers to help the cause along. I hope they will be more effective than the ones we have now.
The bill before us contains some proposals to deal with our environment. According to one press report, it is man's greed that is supposed to be the real culprit responsible for the damage that has been done to our environment. The article goes on to describe the Ottawa River as a flowing sewer which is at the service of a group of pulp companies. This may be so. I am willing to accept the description of it by the hon. member on the government side. What surprises me a little is that it took the government so long to make this finding, since the situation has been evident for a while now. Perhaps ,it took them that long also to find out that greed is necessary to the functioning of the economic system which the people on the government side so fondly

January 29, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
embrace. Why they are so surprised to see it evident in our economy passes my understanding.
The proliferation of departments and the appointment of extra ministers will not change that situation to any degree. A government which can view present unemployment with equanimity will scarcely solve the problem of unemployment by setting up another department. It will scarcely solve the problem I mentioned this morning, namely, that people in my constituency and indeed in other parts of Canada who are thrown out of work and apply for unemployment insurance payments to which they are entitled, find themselves waiting for six, seven or eight weeks before they get benefits.
What is really necessary is to have the departments presently responsible for these matters operate more effectively and efficiently. Sometimes I think the government has fallen prey to its own propaganda, to its own myths, to its own shibboleths. Cabinet ministers think the just society has really arrived. Perhaps if they would take a good sampling of public opinion instead of creating other departments they would do something about the reality in which they live.
I am concerned to some extent about the matter of environment. This bill refers to soil and water. I just wonder if the new minister will be able to work with those ministers who are responsible for agricultural matters in order to bring about a rational land conservation policy. Last spring we had a program which called for the summer fallowing of a great deal of acreage in western Canada. In fact, it forced farmers to summer fallow land for two years in succession. Mr. Speaker, you can scarcely conceive of a policy that would be more destructive of the basic soil on which our agricultural community depends. You can hardly conceive of a policy which would lead to more water and soil erosion than this type of program.
I wonder if the new minister in charge of improving the quality of the environment will be able to meet with his counterparts and take effective action to protect the environment. In view of the way our cities are expanding I wonder if policies can be developed which will enable feed lots and other agricultural enterprises to fit into the urban picture so that all the needs of our people will be met. Too often, large feed lots and other agricultural enterprises are situated close to cities. On occasion the urban spread encircles farms, and then people living within the urban area demand that things like livestock enterprises, which they find unpleasant, should no longer be carried on within that area. This is not the result of planning, and indicates that no decision has been made that this or that area is suitable for this or that purpose. This situation is the result of speculation, of the greed which is described in this article. I very much doubt that those who drew up this bill were much concerned about these sorts of situations which relate to land use.
I am reasonably sure that the government has been fairly ineffective in dealing with pollution. I recall the situation in Manitoba and the mercury pollution which resulted from discharges into the Saskatchewan River system. I am certainly not aware of the federal government acting in concert with Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta to discuss the matter with chemical and other industrial companies. Instead of that happening, the province of Manitoba launched a law suit against pulp companies and chemical companies in the two other provinces. Unless a better approach is made to the pollution problem, the federal government will be ineffective. The incompetence, the do-nothing attitude of the federal government in this field is of real concern.
Then, there is the question of the trade war going on between the provinces, with the province of Manitoba having to launch action in the Supreme Court in order to establish the prerogatives which properly belong to the federal government in the matter of trade. Trade should flow freely across this land, but the federal government seems to have abandoned its responsibilities in this area.
We have one minister in charge of the Wheat Board, Mr. Speaker. He tries very hard to succeed. I have asked him about the problems that exist in connection with the marketing of rapeseed and futures prices. He has said that he will talk with the Grain Exchange. I believe he said he had a letter from the Exchange, but I have not seen it yet. He has said that he will try to correct the inequalities and inequities that exist in the futures market. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, there is some malfunctioning of the system. Today, I raised with him the matter of the spread between the Vancouver future and the future at Thunder Bay, which is some 46i cents per bushel. Anyone who is knowledgeable of the Grain Exchange, or who is even an observer of the commodity exchanges, will know that this is not a good situation. In fact, it indicates a malfunction in the exchange and a distortion of the prices received by the producer and paid by the consumer, whether the consumer be an importer like Japan or a domestic consumer.
Yet, as I say, no effective action has been taken. Are we waiting until some outsider is able to move in to correct the situation? You can only go so far with camouflage and with going through the motions. It is all very well for posters put out by Information Canada to depict a couple of people practically naked, clad only with a couple of maple leaves. You can have your fun with things of this kind; but that is only play acting. That does not come to grips with the realities or the day to day decisions that the people of Canada are trying to make. You know, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) may be enjoying himself very much riding an elephant, a tiger, a turtle, or whatever else he may find convenient for transportation, but those of us who remain here must live with our day to day problems. There is no indication that the government has become seized of the day to day problems relating to the slow-

January 29, 1971

down in the economy, a slowdown that is creating hardships in all walks of life in all parts of Canada. That slowdown was brought on, encouraged and fostered by the people who sit on the government side of the House.
What disturbs me for example is that the minister responsible for agriculture does not seem to know where the government is going or what its objectives are. Let me illustrate what I mean. We are proposing to encourage the production of forage crops in western Canada. We are proposing to increase, through this method, the size of cattle herds and the production of livestock; yet, at the same time, we are encouraging the increased importation of meat from other countries. I am not one who says that we ought to draw a solid circle around Canada and prevent the importation into Canada of food products. That is not a practical suggestion. What I am saying is that the farmers of Canada have a right to know what the government's policy is. They have a right to know what the limitations of that policy are and, before investing millions of dollars in growing forage crops in western Canada and in increasing livestock production in Canada, they have a right to know what the policy of the government is with regard to importations of meat. Then, they can plan and govern themselves accordingly. This they do not know. All we hear when this point is raised are remarks such as, "Well, we stopped some of this importation before, and we may do so again." That sort of policy is at variance with the policies of other countries.
The United States does not absolutely block the entry of meat coming from other countries. That country has established quotas for meat coming from all countries except Canada. It has established such a policy and its producers have a working knowledge of that policy. They know where they are going. That sort of thing needs to be done here and it has not been done. The Government cannot get away with its present careless and ill-defined policies. The Prime Minister cannot get away merely by shrugging his shoulders and saying, "It is not my job to sell wheat." He did not need to tell us that. We knew that. Nevertheless, it is his job, and the job of those who are part of his government, to outline the policies under which we operate.
Under this bill we shall be able to do either very little in regard to the environment or a great deal. All will depend on the thrust and determination of the government of the day. What is done will depend on how determined governments will be to improve the quality of life. It will depend on how determined they are to make this economy work instead of fiddling while Rome burns.

I wish to put some statistics on the record in order to illustrate how important this industry is to the Atlantic provinces. In the province of Newfoundland, 24,000 people are directly employed in the fishing industry out of a total work force of 130,000. In the three Maritime provinces, 31,000 people are directly employed in the fishing industry out of a total work force of 466,000. These figures are taken from 1968 statistics compiled by the Department of Fisheries and Forestry. I put them on the record to illustrate how important this industry is, not only to the province of Newfoundland, but to all the Atlantic provinces of Canada. In the four Atlantic prov-
