The minister stated that the department of fisheries will no longer exist as a department. As he termed it, the Canadian fisheries service of the new department of the environment will rank in terms of importance with the Canadian wildlife service and the Canadian forest service.
The Canadian wildlife service serves a very useful function in the preservation and management of our wild life. The forestry service carries out very useful and efficient work in the field of experimentation in an attempt to combat various diseases in our forests. Neither of the services directly contribute to the Canadian economy to the same extent as the fisheries industry, and I am speaking in the federal context, especially in the Atlantic provinces and the province of British Columbia. I feel that we have cause for concern in the overall context of federal responsibility.
I notice that the appointment of the new deputy minister has already been announced. I understand that he is a professional engineer from Montreal. This man does not have the remotest connection, nor has he ever been
remotely connected, with the fishing industry. This is more evidence of why we are concerned about the downgrading of the fishing industry and the fisheries department in this bill. The department of fisheries is to be a service within the new department similar to the wildlife service. It will be presided over by an assistant deputy minister. I sincerely ask, what is wrong with having two deputy ministers in the department? I made this suggestion to the minister. I will put this suggestion in the form of an amendment at the appropriate time.
If there were two deputy ministers, one could be responsible for the over-all management of our fisheries department and the other could have over-all responsibility for the other areas in the new department. In this way, we would ensure that the responsibilities of Parliament in the areas of management, development and exploitation of Canada's fisheries would receive the attention it so justly deserves. The new deputy minister has been appointed, notwithstanding the fact that this bill is still before the House. I would have at least expected the government to wait the few days necessary for this bill to go through the legislative process, be enacted and become law before announcing the appointment of the new deputy minister.
I wish to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) in paying tribute to the retiring Deputy Minister of Fisheries and Forestry, Dr. Needier. I am happy to note that he will continue to play a role in the department and that he will have a special responsibility in so far as the fishing industry and our international negotiations with respect to conservation are concerned.
There are reasons for concern. They are manifest in the minister's speech and in this bill. I say to the approximately 4,000 Canadians who are presently employed by the Department of Fisheries and Forestry that they better get on the bandwagon or else they will be left out. They better acquaint themselves with the new responsibilities of the minister in the area of pollution and pollution control. As far as this government is concerned, there is not much future in the fishing industry, although the facts and statistics I have put before the House certainly contradict that statement. I do not for a moment want to take anything away from the importance of having effective measures to combat pollution. We all know the seriousness of pollution. We know of the critical stage we have arrived at in this country and in this world. We have polluted our environment to the point at which certain species of wildlife are under threat of extinction. We know that the very survival of man is at stake. Let me repeat that it is necessary and essential that we adopt effective measures of control.
It is logical that we give this responsibility to the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry. He is obviously the man who should have the responsibility for combating pollution. That minister is responsible in respect of our fisheries, and this is an area which is more directly affected by pollution than perhaps any other in Canada.

January 29, 1971

This fact was recognized long before pollution became a popular subject. It was recognized when the Fisheries Act was drawn up many years ago. At that time, adequate provisions were written into the act to combat pollution. Unfortunately, for reasons which have not been sufficiently or adequately explained, these provisions in the Fisheries Act have never been enforced.
When we were amending the Fisheries Act and examining the Canada Water Act we could not find a rational or logical explanation why various ministers of the department of fisheries down through the years did not see fit to enforce the very stringent and strict provisions of this act. We put forward the suggestion when the fisheries Act was last before the House that, in effect, there was no need for a Canada Water Act if the pollution provisions of the Fisheries Act were enforced. The federal government already had the power at the time Parliament enacted the Canada Water Act to combat pollution. The Fisheries Act contains provisions even to this day which, had they been enforced, would have prevented a great deal of the pollution which now exists. The Canada Water Act is much like a toothless tiger. It is ineffective. I do not want to repeat the arguments presented at the time this bill was presented to the House, but it is ineffective to a large degree because it depends upon provincial and municipal initiative. The provinces and municipalities in this country will be motivated and guided by economic considerations. These considerations must be favourable to them before water management areas in Canada are set up to combat pollution.
The Minister of Fisheries, who will inherit jurisdiction for the Canada Water Act as a legacy under this bill is now saying these things, too. But, Mr. Speaker, he is a little late. Let me quote what he is reported as having said as it appears in the Sunday Express of January 3, 1971 under the headline "Whiz-kid Davis Defends Mother Nature". This minister is our knight on a white charger and is reported as follows:
Davis feels the poison chemicals which can kill in even small quantities should be the first target of government attack, and to ban them he'll use the Canada Fisheries Act, not the Canada Water Act which was so recently passed by parliament.
"The Canada Water Act requires federal-provincial-municipal co-operation to work. The law is already there in the Canada Fisheries Act to force clean-ups, and industry is being fairly co-operative"-
We can draw some consolation from the fact the minister is now saying what we said at the time the Canada Water Act was before the House. We can draw precious little consolation from the fact that the time spent considering the Canada Water Act, its preparation, the debate on it and the exhaustive and extensive examination by the committee must be written off as a waste of time. The water act is not yet operative. It has no past, and if what the minister says is an indication, it has no future.
We are asking that this new department created by this omnibus bill now before the House reflect in its name the importance of the fishing industry to the Canadian economy. What is wrong with naming the new
Government Organization Act, 1970 department the department of fisheries and the environment? In that way we might expect the department to live up to its obligations in so far as the fishing industry is concerned. As things now stand, there is a risk that the fishing industry in Canada, which is a responsibility of this Parliament, will lose something in the shuffle.
I suggest that perhaps we should make provision for the appointment of two deputy ministers. I think there is precedent for this suggestion in that we have a deputy minister of health and a deputy minister of welfare within the one department. In the interest of preserving this industry upon which Atlantic Canada is so dependent, I should like to know what is wrong with the suggestion that the word "fisheries" be incorporated in the name of the act. In that way, the federal government's responsibility under our constitution, as recognized at the time of confederation, would be assured. Perhaps we could appoint two special deputy ministers, one responsible for fishing and the other responsible for the environment.
There are other subjects I should like to deal with if time permitted, but I realize a number of other members want to participate in this debate. Members from the Atlantic provinces have some concern about conservation and the establishment of agreements which hopefully can be negotiated in order to provide some kind of agreement on a sustained yield basis in respect of Atlantic fisheries.
We know that negotiations are taking place at this time and that there will be a meeting of the International Commission on North Atlantic Fisheries. I am told that this will be a subject on the agenda of that meeting. It is my view that the Canadian fisheries industry should be adequately protected by meaningful international agreements which will hopefully be worked out by the International Commission on North Atlantic Fisheries when it meets in May of this year.
This morning I read of the formation of a committee in the United States in respect of the preservation of the Atlantic salmon. We have said many times in this House to the Minister of Fisheries and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) that we are concerned about the future of the Atlantic salmon. It is being threatened as a species by the exploitation of one of the member countries, namely, Denmark. It is a well-known fact that within the last ten years Denmark has discovered the North Atlantic salmon feeding grounds. These salmon are hatched in Canadian rivers and protected by Canadian laws. Millions of dollars have been spent to preserve this species of fish, not only as a source of food but as sport fish as well. If the Danes continue to exploit this fish off Greenland at the present rate, then the Atlantic salmon cannot possibly survive as a species beyond the next ten years.
A group of prominent people in the sport fishing industry in the United States recently took some initiative in this connection, and I salute them for it. I only hope a similar initiative will be taken in Canada. In particular, I

January 29, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970 hope the government will tell Denmark in the strongest possible diplomatic language that Canada takes a very dim view of its activities in the over exploitation of Atlantic salmon; that if Denmark does not agree to preserve the species under some sustained yield system, Canada will threaten economic sanctions against them until they do. I have made this suggestion before, as has the hon. member for South Shore, and I now make it again.
We wonder what will become of these urgent and pressing problems faced by the fishing industry once this bill passes the House and this new department of the environment is set up. For our part, we will continue to express our concern in the only way open to us, namely by moving appropriate amendments to the bill when it comes before the committee of the whole House.
Before I take my seat, I want to make one more point. As a member of parliament, I resent very strongly the government putting this bill before the House in its present form. I find there are provisions in the bill that I can support wholeheartedly. On the other hand, I find provisions to which I am very much opposed. Yet, I must take the whole package or I must reject the whole package.
I contend that Members of Parliament should not be placed in this position. This bill deals with many unrelated subjects. I have read Your Honour's ruling and the arguments preceding it, and I acknowledge that there are precedents. But I submit there is no precedent which supports an omnibus bill of this sort that embodies so many different, unrelated subjects, from additional Parliamentary Secretaries to pensions, from setting up a new department of the environment to creating new ministers of state. Members of Parliament should not be placed in this position.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL RE-ORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill has been referred to on a great many occasions as an omnibus bill, a government catch-all or a new bag of tricks. The descriptive part of the bill indicates that this is an act respecting the organization of the government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto. Having read the bill, and also the speech made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), it appears to me to cover the entire waterfront of the government activities. Items dealing with new ministers and Parliamentary Secretaries appear to me to be a backdoor method of increasing the salaries of many of the more vociferous backbenchers on the government side. The fact that during this debate there has been better attendance by these hon. members is an indication that hope is springing eternal in the Grit breasts.
Well, Mr. Speaker, why not? The extra $4,000, even for two years-which of late has been the prescribed life of most Parliamentary Secretaries-would add an extra $2,000 to the yearly salary of a great many government members. A great many of them could be the recipients of this extra income during the lifetime of a Parliament. After all the guff that came out after the announcement that Members of Parliament might get an increase in
salary, this looks to me like a backdoor method of giving a reward to the righteous, so to speak. It is also a method of holding out a carrot before the other poor rabbits as an indication that if they behave themselves they, too, may become Parliamentary Secretaries. A former outspoken cabinet minister in the Liberal party many years ago said: "If we want to get away with it, who's going to stop us?" The same arrogant air of ruling by divine right has once again permeated the front benches of the government.
A few years ago this House was faced with another omnibus bill, the one that created our over-burdened committee system. The failure of that particular scheme as evidenced by the present breakdown of our committee system, cannot help but make this House and the nation skeptical of the effectiveness of this and other schemes. For example, yesterday the committee chairmen and their deputies in both the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs were not prepared to discuss a bill which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) has stated is one of the most important to come before this Parliament this year. The minister was in the House making a speech and had not troubled to find out whether the committee was sitting. As a result the committee had to wait 15 or 20 minutes, wasting the time of members and the witnesses who were to appear. This is just one example of the ineffectiveness of our committee system.
However, most of my remarks will be related to the establishment of a department to be known as the department of the environment. This is a department that members of this party have for many years advocated. Last year when we were discussing the water bill, time after time, both in committee and in the House, members of the official opposition suggested the creation of such a department. I think all the environmental problems that are so prevalent in this country should be placed under the jurisdiction of one minister.
I should like to say that the minister who is going to head this department is, in my estimation, one of the most far-sighted and able ministers. He is probably the one most capable of grappling with this particular question. This is the most redeeming part of this legislation. I understand, of course, the problems facing members from the Maritime provinces, where fishing is such an important part of the economy. These members have indicated that they fear for the fishing industry of Canada if that department is downgraded.
I was a little disturbed when the minister who is going to head this department said in the House the other day that we in Canada must make sacrifices, especially on the economic front, if we want a better world than we have now. It almost seems as if the minister does not feel the time has now come to take action to deal with many of our environmental problems.
Last Friday in this House the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney), when speaking on a bill that had to do with setting aside a national

January 29, 1971

pollution awareness week, had this to say, as reported at page 2690 of Hansard:
-the desire to pinpoint the significance of pollution in ail ways, the significance of the cost of pollution to our environment and to our society, the benefits of controlling and reversing it, and the cost that we must pay in achieving that benefit, must all be made known to the public before emotional steps are taken.
Mr. Speaker, this was brought to the fore by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I refer to an article in the Windsor Star for February 27, 1970, under the heading "Pollution, water: Is Trudeau serious?" I shall read a few excerpts from this editorial to indicate the point I wish to make:
On Wednesday a sizeable audience of Windsor citizens heard health and welfare minister John Munro speak on the necessity for an all-out fight against all forms of pollution. There was even the promise of a clean air act to go with the recently passed Canada Water Act.
All very dandy.
Except that Mr. Munro's boss, Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau, had downgraded current concern about pollution as just another "kick" on Tuesday night when taping a television show with Carleton University students.
This is just another kick people are taking. The article continues:
The PM's remark must also make resources minister J. J. Greene feel a little sick about the Canada Water Act and the considerable trouble Greene has gone to in justifying its necessity when the majority of provinces would rather the federal government left the area of water pollution well enough alone.
Joe Greene was not over having the rug pulled out from under him by the swinging bossman. Mr. Greene had also just made his most unequivocating statement about Canada not selling its water to the United States in the House of Commons.
Lo and behold, there was Mr. Trudeau telling the student audience at the television taping that since Canada can't use all its water it shouldn't be possessive about it. We, of course, should consider selling our resources "for good, hard cash" said the Prime Minister.
This is an indication to me of the feeling of the government at the present time. They hope pollution is something that will go away. It is an indication that the government does not have any immediate plans to control pollution. They fear that the majority of Canadians do not understand. This would seem to be an insult to the credibility of the Canadian people. There have been sit-ins, think-tanks, symposiums and pollution probes at every level of government and its agencies. In fact, the other day when someone spoke of the Ottawa River it was suggested that we have another survey. We have had so many surveys that it is now time for action. Studies by magazines, periodicals, radio and television have all brought home to the public the extremely critical situation we face in connection with our environment. One of the principles of true conservation is that each generation passes on to the next an environment as close as possible to the one he received.
We brag about our affluent society. We certainly have done a dandy job of ruining our environment. Do we have to wait until disease runs rampant throughout our land because of our inability to grapple with our wastes?
Government Organization Act, 1970 Do we have to wait until babies die from air pollution before we do something about our air? Are we to find ourselves running short of arable land, pure water and clear air until one day we find ourselves knee deep in garbage?
One of my first speeches in this House was in the field of conservation. I have always been happy and proud of the fact that one of the first conservation programs was established in my area. I refer to the Grand River conservation program. The main physical structures were built within the confines of my riding. However, the authority that has the responsibility for administering this scheme found itself in difficulty because federal assistance was cut off last year by the repeal of the Water Conservation Assistance Act when the water bill was passed.
The previous act contained a formula whereby the three levels of government participated in projects of this type in the ratio of 37J per cent by the federal government, 37 J per cent by the provincial government and 25 per cent by the municipalities involved. In private conversations I have had with the minister he indicated that he would consider some type of assistance for a water management plan on the Grand River, but until he indicates whether a new formula will be presented, or to what extent the federal government will participate, it is difficult for the responsible body to carry forward its projected plans.

When I attended football games we had a cheer which went like this: Feed them oats, feed them hay, feed them anything but stop that play.
I see no reason why the water act of last year cannot be amended to include the original formula. The Grand River Conservation Commission has plans which, if implemented, could create hundreds of jobs and could be of tremendous assistance to the communities in the area by improving the quality and flow of water so necessary for continued development.
This is only one phase in the improvement of our environment. I see many areas in which government action could be taken by various departments toward improving our environment. For instance, our Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) has laid great emphasis on the necessity of equipping cars with gadgets that would reduce the amount of deleterious material coming from exhausts. The areas where this is most prevalent are the centres of our cities. Many municipalities have installed equipment to measure the pollution content of these areas, and the readings vary to a frightening degree. Recently in a Canada-Japan newsletter an article appeared entitled, "Menace of Pollution Spurs Search for Practical Electric Car". Periodicals and magazines have emphasized the necessity of this type of pollution control, and universities participated in a marathon race across the United States emphasizing the importance of so-called clean car exhaust systems.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has made a great issue of the new packaging bill he has brought forward. But has he brought forward a container or bottle to hold hazardous products which have brought into jeopardy the lives of so many children in Canada? The latest figures show there were 50,000 last year. What has the minister done with regard to throw-away, nonreturnable bottles which have become such a blot on the highways and the streets of our towns and cities? Mr. Speaker, I do not think we have to wait for the people of Canada to become emotionally aroused before we take very rapid and vital steps to eliminate pollution.
Our government is twisting and turning, trying to find ways and means of grappling with the problem of unemployment which finds hundreds of thousands of Canadians in a hopeless, helpless, almost frantic situation as they face not only days and weeks but in some cases years with no hope of steady employment. I have in my hand two or three speeches that were made by the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis). I know he is very interested in these projects and in the solution of this problem. One of his speeches is entitled, "Conservation: a dynamic concept". What we need is a man with dynamic concepts and ideas.

speechtext:
Another speech which the minister made is entitled, "Recycling and recovery: the twin keys to environmental control". Both of these speeches contain a great many ideas regarding ways and means of improving our pollution problem in Canada. Recycling and recovery is something in which I have become very interested. I have here a book entitled, "Garbage as you like it. A plan to stop pollution by using our nation's wastes". It is a very interesting book, well written, in simple language, but it gives some idea of methods used in other parts of the world to dispose of garbage, to recycle it and to segregate it. Garbage can be composted first and then sold as a fertilizer. Paper could be reclaimed and so could metal, to be used in factories to carry on our industrial production.
A few years ago "bold" and "imaginative" were used as a catch-phrase by the Liberal government. If my memory serves me correctly, the government did not prove to be very bold or imaginative. We can survive a monetary crack-up. We can survive a social revolution. We cannot survive the destruction of our environment. It will take bold and imaginative planning, such as the creation of satellite cities on unproductive land rather than the creation of asphalt deserts on our good, arable land. There has been a historic tradition in the Liberal Party of suggestions of this kind. I remember a speech made by a former Prime Minister of this nation, Right Hon. Mackenzie King, shortly after the last war in which he said this would have to be done. At that time they were not sure that wars were over. The same is true today. We know how vulnerable our cities would be if war broke out.
The former minister in charge of housing, who was previously the Minister of National Defence, also had the idea of setting up satellite cities. These are bold and imaginative ideas to move people from crowded areas of the cities to land that is unproductive and where cities could be built and developed. It will take bold and imaginative ideas such as the development of a recycling program for the water in our homes, apartments and places of business.
A couple of years ago there was a great deal of fanfare concerning the building of a house in Rockcliffe where the water was to be recycled. I telephoned the National Research Council recently and was told that this project had been wrapped up because of a couple of problems that arose. If they can recycle the water in swimming pools used by our children in schools, why cannot they recycle the water used in our homes, apartments and other buildings? I maintain that we are not doing enough research in this area. Solutions to these problems will have to be found if we are to survive. Many cities have tried different ways and means, but so many of them result in just moving the problem from one place to another. In other words, incineration fills the area with tons and tons of pollutants which filter down, sometimes not on the city but on some place in the area.
It would seem that some plans have proved effective; they are described in this book. Means have been found of segregating different types of garbage and composting others. Many cities are coming to grips with the problem. I know that in my area, in the last year several municipalities have been having difficulty disposing of

January 29, 1971

their garbage and have united to buy land on which it could be disposed. Further research might indicate means whereby a number of smaller communities could form a composting unit where their garbage could be disposed of in one area. These are problems which have to be solved if we are to avoid destroying our environment.
I think the government should explore the possibility of providing assistance for communities which face such problems. I know that through the National Housing Act assistance can be provided to communities for setting up sewage disposal programs, but I think we have to delve into the problem deeper if we are to accomplish what must be accomplished in order to survive. Many projects that are not completely self-supporting have been helped financially through the sale of fertilizer, paper and metal.
It appears that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has the idea that pollution is not very important in the minds of the people of Canada. I do not think it is necessary to await public approval before taking the bold and imaginative steps which I have suggested to overcome unemployment and many of the environmental problems which our affluent society has created.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak briefly on only one or two of the matters dealt with in this bill. As a matter of fact, if one were to deal with all the proposals in the bill, the limit of 40 minutes on speeches at this stage in our proceedings would have to be stretched. However, the evils of an omnibus bill of this kind have been dealt with by my colleagues and I will only add my protests to theirs against this sort of measure being introduced. This measure is called, "an act respecting the organization of the government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto". The bill might much more properly be entitled, "an act to provide jobs for the boys". That is essentially what it is.
In my opinion, the most important provision in the bill is the one which provides for a considerable increase in members of the cabinet. Up to five ministers of state will have specific jobs to perform. Several other ministers of state will not have specific jobs to perform but will assist the ministers who presently have departments. There will also be ministers without portfolio. At present there are 28 members in the cabinet. With the additions proposed under this bill, there may be anything up to 10, 12 or 15 more. This would make the biggest cabinet of any country in the world.
Our cabinet is already too big. We have 28 ministers looking after the affairs of some 21J million people. Immediately to the south of us is a country with 10 times our population. They have 12 cabinet members, plus the President and the Vice-President-14 people to look after the affairs of a population of some 220 million-ten times ours-and with a great many more international commitments and governmental business of all kinds than we have. It is an absolutely ridiculous situation for us to have a cabinet of 28 people while the United States cabinet numbers 14.
Government Organization Act, 1970
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, rather than increasing the number of cabinet ministers, if this were a reasonable bill we would be cutting the number down to at least half. As a matter of fact, I do not know how they all find a place to sit in the cabinet chamber in the East Block. There is not room for 28 chairs around the cabinet table, so a considerable number of them must sit back in the corner like Little Jack Horner.

speechtext:
There just is not room around the table for them. There may be room in the temporary cabinet chamber, which used to be used for the Progressive Conservative caucus, on the third floor. So long as they use small chairs, they may possibly squeeze 28 around that table, but certainly if the size of the cabinet is increased there would not be room for all the ministers. Somebody says that maybe the cabinet will be run on the roster system. Certainly something will have to be done along that line.
If you examine this measure, Mr. Speaker, you will see that it is one of the most ridiculous proposals ever put before the House. It is a complete waste of public funds. Rather than increasing efficiency in government, it is bound to decrease efficiency. A cabinet of 28 is too large. A cabinet of 28 cannot operate efficiently. If you are to have a dictatorial form of government with a Prime Minister and two or three of his close colleagues running it, it does not matter if you have a cabinet of 300. But if you are to have cabinet government, which I think is the best form of government, you need a cabinet of manageable proportions-and a 28-member cabinet is not that. Increase the size of the cabinet by 10 or 15 ministers and it becomes a completely hopeless situation. We will not have cabinet government; we will have a dictatorial form of government with the Prime Minister and two or three of his cronies running it and the rest of the cabinet being more or less nonentities. I protest as strongly as I can against an innovation of this kind.
If the government was intent on introducing effective cabinet reorganization, it should have looked at the British system where there is a cabinet of anywhere from 12 to 15 ministers, with a number of junior ministers who look after administrative functions of various kinds. That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing a measure to amend the Income Tax Act to provide that where a student, enrolled at an educational institution, is entitled to deduct his tuition fees in computing his income for a taxation year, he may also deduct expenses paid by him for textbooks, laboratory equipment or charges in respect thereof, student union fees, medical fees, athletic board fees and other expenditures necessary for or incidental to enrolment at the educational institution; and similarly, that a taxpayer, whether the spouse or otherwise the student, who pays such tuition fees and other such expenses, whether in whole or in part, upon behalf of the student, may deduct any amounts so paid in computing his income for a taxation year.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members who have allowed their motions to stand in order that I may discuss this measure which I think is of concern to everybody in this House and in the country.
My motion really is in two parts. The first part gives a student the right to deduct tuition fees as expenses from moneys earned to provide for a college or university education. It also provides for the deduction of expenses incurred in respect of laboratory equipment, textbooks, etc. The most important feature relates to the right of a taxpayer, generally the parent, who has committed himself to putting a daughter or son through college or university. This expense should be allowable as a deduction from income tax.
In order to arrive at a conclusion on this matter it would be helpful to put on record the cost of education in Canada, which is mounting every year. I checked these figures this morning and they are the latest available. The estimated total cost of education in Canada is $6,674,706,000, or $6.6 billion in round figures-in other words, about half the total federal budget in Canada today, which is around $13 billion. The cost of higher education at Canadian universities amounts to $1,602 million. This gives the House an idea of the costs we are talking about.

I want to speak a little on the motion. It is worth pointing out that the government does permit deductions, and has since 1961, for that part of a student's university fee that is clearly related to his studies. The plea which the hon. member for Calgary North makes is that this be extended to include other items in the category of student fees in order to give the student additional income tax deductions.
I have some figures here which are worth noting and which give an idea of the size of the present deduction. Perhaps from that we can get an idea of the total sum involved. In 1968, the deduction in respect of tuition fees, based on all taxation returns, amounted to about $111 million. On the basis of taxable returns, the amount was about $81 million. You can estimate from that that in the year 1968 the cost to the federal and provincial governments which did not receive that revenue was in the order of $20 million. So we are looking at $20 of revenue which federal and provincial governments forgo in respect of only that portion of the fees which relates to studies. How much more of these fees is unrelated to studies, I am not quite sure. It varies from department to department in the university and it depends on the extent to which the student involves himself in all sorts of student activities. Some of these are obligatory, such as alma mater fees and the like, while athletic fees and fees of other kinds are not.
In any event, we can estimate that if the whole package were deductible, it could go up perhaps by another 25 per cent to 50 per cent and we would be looking at revenue losses of the order of $20 million or $30 million spread over the 400,000 university students in Canada today. It is not really a very significant sum. However, there are many other ways in which we can assist universities through the federal government.
When we come to these comparisons it is interesting to note a tendency which exists. I think the hon. member for Calgary North will concur in what I am about to say. When the federal government starts to support a university through one device or another, the province in which the university is located takes a look at its annual budget and the amount of money it pays to the university, and the provincial Minister of Finance shrugs and says, "Look at the federal treasury putting all that money in. I

I know that in my own province of British Columbia this was very evident a few years ago when Dr. Bladen of the University of Toronto brought down his report on university financing, a report which was commissioned by the universities of Canada. It demonstrated clearly the tendency of provincial Ministers of Finance, when they see a federal windfall coming, not to let the benefit accrue fully to the university by cutting down their own budgets. So whatever we do in this direction, let us do it remembering that not all the funds will pass directly into the hands of the universities but some will be taken away from them before they ever get there.
In what other ways does the federal government assist the universities of Canada? It is estimated that in 1969-70 the advances to the provinces for post-secondary education were $625 million, or about two-thirds of $1 billion. Student loans, which were mentioned earlier in the debate today, in 1969-70 amounted to $80 million and they went to 130,000 students. If we look at the full statistics on this we find that the outstanding value of student loans as of June, 1970, was $237 million, of which the federal government was paying interest on $163 million. This is a very considerable contribution to the young people of this country who are looking for help in financing their studies.
The Canada Council assists universities in a number of ways, particularly through its capital fund which, hon. members will remember, was originally set at $50 million and to which additional funds have been added. At the University of British Columbia, in my own constituency, funds of the Canada Council went a long way toward the expansion of the university library and some went into student housing. I note that at the University of B.C., which had a considerable building program for student housing, $5J million from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation went into construction that year. We expect an equivalent amount go into the completion of that construction in the current year. As a result, the student who is housed in these quarters is housed at a much cheaper rate than he would be outside. The effect is to reduce the amount which can be charged locally because of the influence of rates on the campus and rates which are established in relation to the amount of funds they are able to borrow from sources such as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Of course, the government has involved itself on campuses across Canada in a number of very sizeable scientific laboratories and scientific developments, including the new Triumf development at the University of B.C., which is a nuclear experimental laboratory of important dimensions. There is another area of support which is extremely important to us in reviewing the total picture of what we can do for the student in order to make it possible for him to secure his education. That is in the field of jobs for students during the summer time. I was heartened to learn that $50 million is to be made available this summer for youth programs. I hope all that money will not be spent on buses and gasoline, as suggested by the Globe and Mail, and that some will trickle off to youth and students who are attempting to educate themselves. But it is not really on crash projects such as this that we must count. We must count on annual programs, programs which year after year will sustain students who go out and try to earn enough money in order to go back to university in the fall.
I have always felt that the federal government could do much more than it does now to establish a well co-ordinated program, drawing on the resources of many departments and using them to assist students in summertime. I want to suggest some guidelines which the government might think about with respect to such a program. First, the program be well co-ordinated. Second, it should give summer employment over a long time. Many of these programs are so short in length that they are not totally effective for the student who has to work in the summertime. Third, these programs should pay real wages and not just toy wages. Very often when a student looks at a government program that is offered to him he says, "That's just dandy, if all I wanted was popcorn money. If that is all I wanted I would take the job, but I have to put some money away in order to go back to university next year." We should look at the wage scale we are paying students if we expect these programs to do any good.
The jobs offered to students should not be petty little ticket-taking jobs at the gates of our national parks. I think that a student's work in the summer ought to be related to his knowledge, his education and his skills, so that he will reach the end of summer with a wad of money in his pocket, ready to return to university and feeling he has put in a useful summer being a good Canadian citizen and doing a useful job. I think a student's job should have some real purpose in building Canada. The summer should be a time during which we are doing surveys of all kinds, doing work on the Indian reserves, perhaps doing a lot of those things that other agencies in the past have tried and which the Canada Council has only loused up.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to be very brief in my comments. Essentially, the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), through advocating the device of making expenses incurred in the course of obtaining an education deductible for income tax purposes, has the effect of lightening the financial burden now being sustained by students and the families of students enrolled in educational institutions. I believe it to be an imaginative, interim step toward the removal of all financial obstacles which stand in the way of the complete fulfilment of each individual in our society, in so far as education contributes to the fulfilment of the individual. The suggestion is especially relevant at this point in Canada's history, with unemployment being astronomically high, because it is becoming increasingly difficult for students to find the kind of summer employment they require in order to have wherewithall to return to school in the fall.
One might have hoped that the hon. member for Calgary North in preparing his resolution would have proposed to the government the total elimination of financial obstacles standing in the way of the achievement of an education, but I expect that he formulated this resolution in the least radical way in order to make it more palatable to the conservative tastes of hon. gentlemen sitting opposite on the government benches.
I think the economic pay-offs of encouraging the development of an increasingly well educated population have been well documented within the last few years by studies such as those conducted by the Economic Council of Canada. I also believe there can be no doubt in the mind of any hon. member that financial considerations have a considerable influence upon the amount of formal education which Canadians seek and receive. For example, studies have demonstrated an almost directly proportional relationship between the income of a student's parents and the frequency with which his university education has been interrupted. I suspect that similar relationship could be established with respect to other post-secondary institutions if similar studies were undertaken.
To the degree that the provisions of this resolution would contribute to the removal of financial obstacles to a person's obtaining the best education of which he is capable, it is worthy of the support of this chamber as a recommendation to the government for action, and on that basis I would support the resolution. However, if I may I should like to introduce another area for thought into these deliberations.
It has been the experience of jurisdictions that have chosen to make education at all levels available to their citizens without cost, and even in those jurisdictions which offer considerable financial incentives to their citizens to pursue their education, that the successful pursuit of post-secondary education remains largely an achievement of the middle and upper classes and that the
participation of lower-income groups in the programs is only marginally higher than it is in those jurisdictions which offer no such financial encouragement.
Since it is a demonstrable fact that native intelligence levels amongst the children of lower-income groups are distributed in exactly the same manner as they are amongst the children of the middle and upper-income groups, it would appear that a major part of the problem is one of motivation, the degree of assumption of success on the part of children, the level of expectations of children and the ability of middle-class teachers to deal in an adequate fashion with the education of lower-income students. I suggest that this question of motivation and the means of developing it is an area to which the House could profitably devote some of its attention in the near future.
In saying this, I am not suggesting to hon. members that it would not be a worth-while measure to remove all remaining financial obstacles to education-to use a shorthand phrase, making education at all levels and in all categories free. What I am saying is that if there is to be such a program and this is the way in which we should be moving, we need to develop concurrently with such a program a means of developing the kind of motivation amongst all our citizens which would enable them to avail themselves of the program with some prospect of success.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to support this motion proposed by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). One of the things we most certainly should do is encourage self-help among the young people. I do not object to spending money to be used in education, especially when it is spent well. Nevertheless, it would be only fair if we could relieve the burden of those Canadians who already are paying too much in taxes in this regard. I am talking about middle-income Canadians. They are already carrying a triple burden of taxation. They already pay heavily in taxation if they own their own home, as most of them do. They carry the burden of education; taxes levied against their properties pay for education. I know about this: I pay $700 in taxes every year on a bungalow in a village. I do not object to that because I think the money is well spent. Nevertheless, there comes a limit in our ability to pay. Relief must be given, in view of present living costs, for those with children going to high school or university.
Obviously, if you make $10,000 a year you cannot ask for welfare or assistance of any kind; you can only ask

for equity in taxation, and I claim we are not getting that. Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of attention to the speech made by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wool-liams). I commend him for bringing this matter forward. I must also criticize him, because his motion does not deal with the problem of equalizing educational opportunities in Canada. Those who represent the rural parts in Canada, the areas far removed from universities, know that the main cost of educating our young people is not the cost of tuition; indeed, that may be considered as being one of the smaller parts of the cost. The main cost lies in the burden of sending the student to university and bringing him back. As I say, the main cost is not the cost of tuition but the cost of room and board as well as the cost of transporting the student to and from university. He must go to university, return home at Christmas, go back to university and then come home at other times. In these latter areas lies the real cost.
If we are interested in doing as the hon. member for Calgary North suggests, of equalizing some of the costs of education and making education more equitable and available for a greater number of students then, it seems to me, we must concentrate in those areas I have mentioned, the costs involved in sending a student to university and in maintaining his room and board. I have raised
Income Tax Act
this matter, since coming here in 1965, several times with ministers of finance. Every time they have said to me, "What about students who live in cities and choose to live in residence? Should they not also expect to obtain relief through these tax deductions?" My answer to that has been a simple and unequivocal no. Those people have a choice. The student coming from outside the city has no choice. If he wishes to further his education, he simply must pay for his room and board.
Generally speaking, the incomes of the parents of children in rural communities, who wish to send their children on for further training or education, are lower than those of parents in urban centres. Therefore, a student who goes into a city to attend university, obtain postsecondary education, or even attend school, is at a disadvantage when compared with his urban counterpart. It seems to me that in the white paper tax reforms which the minister is proposing, special note ought to be taken of this discrimination which adversely affects students coming from the rural areas of Canada.
It can be safely said, for example, that for the tax dollar which the rural taxpayer pays to the federal government he probably receives less value than he receives in return, in comparison with any other dollar he may spend. The reason for that is not hard to see. When we go to rural areas we can see just how many federal and provincial government offices are there, compared with the number of such offices in urban communities. According to the 1961 census, the people of my riding finish school either at grades 5 or 6. That is their average educational level. The difficulties of such people in dealing with the bureaucracy of the federal government or provincial governments are almost insuperable, because they simply do not have the education or confidence that one needs to deal with bureaucrats in Ottawa or in any other urban centre.
Although we are prepared to accept some diminution in the return on our tax dollar in the field of education, we protest against the kind of discrimination that is now practised against us, a discrimination arising from the way in which the federal government has arranged for tax deductions to apply solely for tuition without taking into account the most important costs involved in higher education. It is all very well to talk about the crippling burdens that tuition places on the student when in fact about 80 per cent of the costs of higher education is now borne by the general taxpayer. It is borne by individuals, for example, who are not married, by people such as the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Faulkner) and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson), neither of whom has taken the plunge into marriage. Yet both of them are supporting the education of my progeny and of yours, Mr. Speaker.

I was interested in the remark of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman), who said the money made available by the federal government is diverted to other things which the provincial governments may consider more important. I recall when these grants were first made available five years ago, the province of Ontario was accused of cutting the amount of money being paid to universities and using it to build roads. This may have been an admirable social objective but it was not in keeping with the means or purposes for which the money was made available. Because of this kind of fiscal irresponsibility, if the federal government is to ensure that the money goes to the proper place it must engage in the difficult practice of shared-cost programs. Everyone must share the blame and no one must share the credit, to ensure that the moneys go to the proper place.
Under the terms of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act of 1967, the federal government agreed to transfer substantial tax revenues and to make an equalized grant to the provinces. In exchange, the provinces accepted full responsibility for supporting postsecondary education, which requires at least junior matriculation for entrance. To enable the provinces to meet this responsibility the federal government transferred four percentage points of personal income tax and one percentage point of corporate income tax to the provinces. In addition, a post-secondary educational adjustment payment was added, to bring the total transfer up to the greater of $15 per capita of the residents of that province or 50 per cent of the operating costs of post-secondary education in the provinces.
In the last fiscal year for which I have been able to obtain figures, the fiscal transfer and cash adjustment payments for 1969-70 were over $625 million. That money must be paid by the federal government which has no control over the accounting procedures or the way in which budgets are set; the provincial governments merely submit their bills. By the terms of the act and agreement, the federal government must pay. In addition, the federal government provides substantial assistance to students through the student loans plan and grants by the Canada Council and others. In the year 1969-70, approximately $80 million in loans was authorized for over 135,000 students in post-secondary institutions. The value of the loans outstanding as of June 30, 1970, was $237 million on which the government was paying interest on $163 million.

Before I sit down and, hopefully, close the debate I want to reiterate the peculiar financial disadvantages faced by people in northwestern Ontario and other rural parts of Canada. The benefits which the federal government makes available for higher education are considerable. Grants paid to institutions go a long way in making higher education available for more people than ever before. However, a significant amount of the total cost of higher education must still be met by the rural people of Canada through expenses such as room and board. A very expensive part of their education must be borne directly by the parents and students concerned.
I suggest that a way to equalize the direct cost to the students and their parents would be to permit them, where there is taxable income, to write off the costs of transportation and room and board. As a student from a small community who attended university, I can testify as to the expense and the financial difficulties. It would be pleasant if the government provided a surprise in the White Paper tax legislation to allow these additional deductions.
